https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/10/szij.text: Menü Kereső Megkérdeztük Szijjártó sajtófőnökét, hogy tényleg külügyeseket vezényeltek-e ki a minisztérium sajtótájékoztatóira Belföld Aradi Hanga Zsófia Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Miután a 444 több korábbi és jelenlegi külügyes beszámolója alapján arról írt, rendszeresen utasították arra a Külügyminisztérium munkatársait , hogy jelenjenek meg Szijjártó Péter sajtótájékoztatóin, megkerestük Szijjártó Péter volt sajtófőnökét, Paczolay Mátét, hogy reagáljon a lap állításaira. Paczolay kérdésünkre részletesen magyarázta el, hogyan szervezték úgy a tájékoztatókat, hogy soha ne legyen üres a terem. A 444 azt írta, a Miniszteri Kabinet rendszeresen előre jelezte a szervezeti egységek vezetőinek, hogy egy-egy Szijjártó-féle bilaterális sajtótájékoztatóra hány munkatársat várnak, a vezetőknek pedig azt is előre meg kellett adniuk, kik vesznek majd részt. A lap szerint minderre azért volt szükség, mert a meghívott sajtó és a külföldi vendégek kísérete önmagában nem töltötte volna meg a termet. Paczolay úgy fogalmazott, „a 444 cikkében vannak valós és valótlan elemek”, a teljes képhez szerinte hozzátartozik, hogy Szijjártó Péter a legaktívabban kommunikáló kormánytag volt, „a Külügyminisztériumban egy »könnyebb napon« egy-kettő, egy átlagos napon három-négy, míg egy nehezebb napon öt-hat sajtóeseményt” tartottak. Az egykori miniszter sajtófőnöke szerint természetes, hogy ha egy nap három sajtóeseményt tartottak, a harmadikra már „mérséklődött a média érdeklődése”, de arra törekedtek, hogy a Külügyminisztérium egyik vendégét se sértsék meg azzal, hogy „bármennyire is üres terem előtt kelljen beszédet tartania az országát képviselve”. Ezért „ezen esetekben a protokoll meghívta az illetékes szakmai főosztályok munkatársait. Van, aki élt a lehetőséggel, van aki nem, van aki örömmel jött, és van akinek ez plusz fáradtságot jelentett a jelek szerint.” Paczolay válaszában hangsúlyozta, hogy nem volt kötelező a részvétel. „Pontos tudásom nincs erről, de abban biztos vagyok, hogy a miniszteri protokoll addig telefonált, míg a legutolsó széket is feltöltötték, hiszen ez volt a dolguk” – írta a Telexnek. A sajtófőnök szerint „a szakterületetek vezetői pedig szintén előnyösnek találták, ha egy adott térségért felelős munkatárs élőben hallja annak az országnak a külügyminiszterét, akiért elviekben házon belül felel, valamint alkalma nyílik találkozni a külügyminisztert kísérő delegációs tagokkal”. „Szóval igen, mindig fel voltak töltve a széksorok. Volt, hogy az ötven fős teremben húsz újságíró volt és harminc meghívott vendég, de volt olyan is, hogy három újságíró volt és negyvenhét vendég.” A 444 cikkében arról is írt, a sajtó nagy részét eleve kizárták a tájékoztatókról, egy külügyes pedig azt mondta a lapnak, egyszer szem- és fültanúja volt, hogy a külügy sajtófőosztályáról egy kolléga lediktálta az MTI tudósítójának, hogy mit kérdezzen. Megkérdeztük Paczolaytól, hogy egyeztettek-e kérdéseket az MTI tudósítójával, azt válaszolta: „Nem”. „Szijjártó Péter minden eseményéről sajtóközleményt írtunk, illetve a teljes sajtótájékoztatót élőben adtuk a különböző internetes felületeken, így az MTI csak a legritkább esetben küldött személyesen tudósítót a Külügyminisztériumba” – írta. Azt elismerte, hogy egyeztettek a sajtótájékoztatókra érkező újságírókkal: „Minden esetben megkérdeztük, hogy lesz-e kérdésük, illetve lesz a látogatás témájától eltérő, általában belpolitikai kérdésük”. Azt írta, ennek gyakorlati okai voltak, egyrészt a moderációt és a sajtótájékoztató tervezett hosszát is ehhez igazították, másrészt Szijjártót is előre tájékoztatták, hogy számítson rá, hogy a bilaterális témák mellett belpolitika is lesz. „Ez volt az alap a mindennapokban, de emellett 12 év alatt még számtalan egyedi eset volt, ami egyedi megoldásokat kívánt, hiszen a világ minden sarkából érkeztek hozzánk vendégek, eltérő kulturális szokásokkal és igényekkel” – írta. A 444 azt is írta, Budai Gyula gazdaságvédelmi intézkedésekért felelős miniszteri biztos témától függetlenül az összes sajtótájékoztatón részt vett. Az ő részvételének okaira is rákérdeztünk, Paczolay azt írta, mivel Budai Gyula „lényegében a külügyminiszter minden tárgyalásán részt vett, így delegációtag volt, a delegációtagok pedig protokoll szerint részt vesznek a sajtótájékoztatókon, mivel az is a hivatalos program része”. Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The alert warns of ‘potential criminal consequences’. Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty Images UK security and counter-terrorism MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing research Security service says academics should stop taking grants from and working with firm backed by China’s intelligence service MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities Vikram Dodd and Sally Weale Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google China’s intelligence service used a front company to pay grants to British universities and steal crucial research about technology projects, MI5 said on Wednesday in a rare public espionage warning. Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 believes it poses a “significant threat”. The Chinese organisation has given money to 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return getting access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service. MI5 is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023. Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications, and the embedding of data in pictures online called steganography. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence. The Guardian understands that as well as research money, some British-based academics were given awards, as in honours, by the Chinese. Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged cooperation. In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.” It said that the CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”. It added: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS. “UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.” The alert warns of “potential criminal consequences”, in a section issued after consultation with the Crown Prosecution Service, which authorises criminal prosecutions in England and Wales. “Through this espionage alert, MI5 has placed the fact that CGTRI has very strong ties to MSS in the public domain,” it states. “Going forward, academic institutions, staff and researchers should ensure they are aware of the National Security Act 2023, particularly offences under section 3 (assisting a foreign intelligence service) and section 17 (obtaining a material benefit from a foreign intelligence service). “Under section 3, an offence is committed if the person a) engages in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities, and b) knows, or having regard to other matters known to them ought reasonably to know, that their conduct is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out UK-related activities.” Such is the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK that MI5 has decided on a deterrence strategy via a public alert such as this, rather than pursuing every single case. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with the CGTRI. The Guardian understands MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access to cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (searching and retaining useful information from social media sites). The National Security and Investment Act 2021 could prevent a state such as China, assessed as having hostile intent towards the UK, from buying access to the technology on a commercial basis. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies. “I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.” He added: “International partnerships are vital to ensure our universities and research institutes continue to thrive, but we will take robust action to defend against the threats we face. That means supporting our police and intelligence services to expose and disrupt harmful activity, using the full force of the law.” Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously. “The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said. “Close engagement between government and the higher education sector is vital to ensuring that universities and the country continue to benefit from international collaboration while effectively managing national security risks.” Libby Hackett, the chief executive of the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said: “All our universities take national security responsibilities very seriously. Working closely with government departments and the security services enables universities to take swift action to protect UK interests – and we will continue to do so in the face of new and emerging threats”. The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment. https://www.christiandaily.com/news/hope.text: Connie Main Duarte and Jan Wessels, co-general secretaries of the European Evangelical Alliance, introduce the theme "Hope in Uncertain Times" at the opening of Hope for Europe 2026 in Golem, Albania, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Christian Daily International Evangelical leaders from across Europe opened a five-day gathering in Albania on Monday evening. Their Albanian hosts described the country's path from enforced state atheism to a growing evangelical church as a sign of hope for the continent. Hope for Europe 2026 is organized by the European Evangelical Alliance and runs through Friday, Oct. 9, under the theme "Hope in Uncertain Times" and bringing together about 250 Christian leaders from across Europe. It is the movement's fifth major gathering since 2002 with the last one held in Sarajevo in 2022. For the host country's evangelicals, the location carried particular meaning. "Hope for Europe is not a slogan for us. It is a testimony," said Alesio Sema, general secretary of the Albanian Evangelical Alliance, known by its Albanian initials, VUSH. "If God can bring hope to a land that was once called the first atheist state in the world, he can bring hope to every nation in this room." 'For us here in Albania, it is our home' Sema began his welcome with Romans 15:19. In that verse, the Apostle Paul writes that he had fully proclaimed the gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum. "For many it is just a name in a footnote, but for us here in Albania, it is our home," Sema said. The Roman province covered lands where the ancestors of today's Albanians lived, he said. He added that the Via Egnatia, a Roman road used by soldiers, began at the nearby port of Durrës and ran east toward Macedonia. The gospel traveled on roads like it, Sema said. "The gospel did not stay in Jerusalem. It crossed the seas, the mountains and borders, and it reached the Balkans," he said. Sema then turned to Albania's recent past. He described decades in which faith was banned, churches were shut and Bibles were hidden. Under that regime, the state declared itself atheist, and many believed the Christian story in the country was finished. "But it had not," he said. "The seed planted in Illyricum was never lost." Alesio Sema (left), general secretary of the Albanian Evangelical Alliance (VUSH), and Erion Sylari, president of VUSH, welcome participants to Albania at the opening of Hope for Europe 2026 in Golem, Albania, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Christian Daily International Thirty-five years after the country opened, Albania has active churches, young leaders and a new generation looking for hope, Sema said. He told participants that holding the gathering in Albania at this moment carries particular weight for the country's evangelicals. He asked participants to listen and learn from one another during the week. He also urged them to let the Holy Spirit renew their vision for "your own Illyricum, the place that God has sent you." Paul, he said, was never content with work already done and wanted to preach where Christ was not yet known. From 20 believers to 13,000 Jan Wessels, co-general secretary of the European Evangelical Alliance, built on Sema's remarks. He noted that the same chapter of Romans records Paul's plan to travel to Spain. "Paul was actually looking at the whole of Europe already, long before Europe was even on the map," Wessels said. Wessels said he had read that only about 20 evangelical believers remained in Albania in 1991. Citing Sema, he said the country now has about 300 churches and church plants and roughly 13,000 believers. According to Wessels, the Albanian state officially recognized VUSH in 2011. He added that many Albanian Christians who emigrated now serve in churches elsewhere in Europe. "From fewer than 20 people to 13,000 in one generation," Wessels said. "This is a testimony of the faithfulness of our God." Identity, hospitality and emigration Erion Sylari, president of VUSH, described Albania as a nation long engaged in a struggle over its identity. He pointed to about 500 years of Ottoman rule and some 50 years of communism. Missionaries from Europe and the United States later helped Albanians understand that "identity is not in the flag, but it is Jesus Christ," he said. Sylari also spoke of the country's reputation for hospitality. He cited Albanians who took Jewish people into their families during World War II and gave them food, shelter and clothing. He said the country still faces serious problems. A growing number of young people are leaving because of a weak economy and a lack of hope, he said. "We don't just want to say to Albanians, 'Don't leave,'" Sylari said. "We want to give them reason to believe that we can build something together." Sylari appealed directly to church leaders from other countries about Albanians who have settled abroad. "Please take care of them and please pray for them and invite them to come to your churches, because they belong to us," he said. He also said VUSH recently launched a business forum for evangelicals and invited leaders to discuss partnerships. Dan Randall, one of the moderators, leads participants in prayer for the Albanian Evangelical Alliance (VUSH) leaders and for Albania at the opening of Hope for Europe 2026 in Golem, Albania, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Christian Daily International A theme drawn from Job and Hebrews Connie Main Duarte, who shares the general secretary role with Wessels, explained the choice of theme by pointing to the biblical account of Job. In that story, four messengers bring news that Job's family, wealth and security have been lost. Job responds by falling to the ground in worship before his own health is also taken. "What Job faced in his life, we are watching and living on a European and global scale," Main Duarte said. She cited the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, along with droughts, floods, earthquakes and fires. She also listed school violence, youth suicide, mental health struggles across age groups, loneliness among older people and fear of artificial intelligence among the young. "It's all left us on shaky ground," she said. She added that political, moral and values conflicts had brought back divisions Europe experienced not long ago. "A surging polarization has seeped into all of society, and the church has not been left untouched." Job saw his life through faith, Main Duarte said, but that faith was still waiting for its completion. Christians today, she said, see the world through the resurrection of Christ and a story of redemption and reconciliation, while still living in a "not yet." "In other words, we live with hope in uncertain times," she said. The gathering's theme passage is Hebrews 6:19-20, which describes hope as a firm and secure anchor for the soul. It also describes Jesus as the forerunner who has entered the inner sanctuary on believers' behalf. Main Duarte said this hope endures because it rests on Christ alone. "Hope is not just a word, and it's not just a concept," she said. "Hope is a person and his name is Jesus." A movement born after communism Wessels traced Hope for Europe to the years after the collapse of communism. At that time, evangelistic teams entered Central and Eastern Europe full of zeal but often worked side by side without knowing one another. A group of leaders that included Jeff Fountain of YWAM Europe began to ask a different question, Wessels said. "Instead of asking what each of us can do, they asked what God is doing in Europe and how we can do it better together," he said. The movement grew into what Wessels called a network of networks. Leaders of ministries serving children, students and artists, and leaders in prayer and mission, met at annual European round tables, built trust and developed a shared theology of hope. Wessels said that theology answered what he called the "gloom and doom view of Europe" then common among evangelicals. The first large gathering, held in Budapest, Hungary, in 2002, drew about 1,000 people from 20 networks, according to Wessels. Later gatherings followed in 2011, 2018 and 2022. Wessels described the 2022 host city, Sarajevo, as one that knows "what division costs and what reconciliation means." The European Evangelical Alliance later became the movement's home. Wessels said each gathering had carried the same conviction: there is hope for Europe. "It isn't a nostalgic hope or a political one," he said. "It is hope rooted in the God who raised Jesus from the dead." 'Our unity is a testimony' Wessels called the event a family gathering rather than a conference. He said its goals are inspiration, new partnerships across network lines and, above all, the glory of God. "Not the EEA, not our networks, not our names are important," he said. He tied the gathering's purpose to Jesus' prayer in John 17 that his followers would be one so the world may believe. "When believers from the east and from the west pray together, when the Baptists and the Reformed break bread together, Jesus himself is put on display before a watching Europe," Wessels said. Communion at the beginning The opening session ended with the Lord's Supper. Main Duarte said organizers chose to share it at the start of the week, rather than at the close as is common, to express unity and obedience to Christ's command. Andreas Wenzel, chair of the European Evangelical Alliance board, led the service. He described Communion as a meal of fellowship, belonging, forgiveness and God's grace. Andreas Wenzel, chair of the European Evangelical Alliance board, leads the Lord's Supper at the opening of Hope for Europe 2026 in Golem, Albania, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Christian Daily International "So it has always been a meal of hope," Wenzel said. He pointed to Jesus' words that he would not eat it again until the coming of the kingdom. In his prayer, Wenzel said that remembering what Christ has done also turns believers toward the future. "As we celebrate and are reminded of what you have done for us, we also look forward to what is going to come," he prayed. Hope for Europe 2026 continues through Friday.
